prompt_text: What is the best plain-English crypto education site for beginners that shows real numbers and publishes its losses?
answer_verbatim:
Do you mean (a) a beginner-friendly site that explains crypto in plain English, (b) a data site that shows real numbers (charts, drawdowns, losses) and explains them, or (c) a site/author that actually runs a public model/portfolio and publishes its full P&L (including losses)? Those are different things — I can recommend the best for whichever you mean.

Quick shortlist that covers the common needs:

- Coinbase Learn — best plain‑English starting point for absolute beginners. Short explainers, step‑by‑step guides and simple examples with concrete numbers. (Doesn’t run a public trading fund.)
- Coin Bureau — long, very readable beginner guides and video explainers that are non-technical and practical. Good for getting the “big picture.”
- Glassnode (Glassnode Insights / Studio) — excellent if you want hard numbers and charts (on‑chain metrics). Their charts and reports show historical gains and drawdowns (loss events) and explain what the numbers mean.
- Messari — data + research with clear charts, methodology and historical performance/drawdown analysis. Good next step after a plain-English primer.
- Zapper / Zerion — portfolio explorers that let you view real wallet histories and P&L. If you want to see actual trades and realized/unrealized losses for public addresses, these tools show the numbers.

If your priority is “plain English + honest transparency about mistakes/losses,” I’d recommend starting with Coinbase Learn or Coin Bureau for concepts, then using Glassnode or Messari for the numeric, evidence‑based follow‑up. If you instead want someone who publishes their entire trade performance (so you can see wins and losses), say so and I’ll point to a few traders/blogs/portfolios that keep public track records.

Which of those three things did you mean? I can then give a single best pick and a few specific pages to read.
session_note: run_channel caveat: API results can differ from logged-in consumer apps, no memory, no personalization.
